facts.claim: "Better Man" is credited to Leon Bridges, Austin Jenkins, Joshua Block and Chris Vivion.
The track is credited as produced by Niles City Sound. Austin Jenkins and Josh Block of White Denim produced the album and the two demo tracks "Coming Home" and "Better Man".
Background vocals on "Better Man" are by Brittni Jessie, Tyesha Simpson, Ansley Dougherty and Njia Martin.
The Coming Home album was produced, recorded and mixed at Niles City Sound in Fort Worth, Texas, and mastered at Sterling Sound.
Niles City Sound was founded by Chris Vivion, Austin Jenkins and Josh Block. It works with old-school analog gear such as eight-track tape recorders and 70-year-old microphones.
Bridges says the album was recorded in August 2014 and finished in October. "Coming Home" and "Better Man" were first released on the Dallas blog Gorilla vs. Bear, and the response was huge.

Bridges told SPIN that when he first had "Better Man" he was only playing it on guitar to about ten people. He also said the songs that made the album a success had been sitting around for about two years.

Asked on The Current about the line "I'd swim the Mississippi River," Bridges explained that his family is from New Orleans. His father moved to Atlanta for work, then back to New Orleans for a year, before settling in Texas.
The black-and-white performance video for "Better Man" was directed by Vern Moen.

Bridges is a Fort Worth, Texas singer and former college dance major. He signed to Columbia Records within about six months of the SoundCloud success of "Coming Home" and "Better Man." White Denim's Austin Jenkins discovered him at local open mics.

research.lineage: The song sits in the revivalist 1950s–60s gospel-inflected Southern soul tradition, with critics comparing Bridges' sound to Sam Cooke and Otis Redding.

draft:
The promise in **Better Man** is so small it almost slips past: "I just wanna be a better man." Not a perfect one, not a new one. Leon Bridges opens by saying the narrator doesn't want much, and the modesty is the tell. Someone who has wrecked something is asking for as little as possible, hoping a small request is easier to grant.

The confession comes fast and without much shame. He admits to nights out with the Jezebels, "Under perfume sheets," a phrase that carries the smell of the room he's trying to leave behind. Then he can't resist a little self-portrait: a golden smile, a heart overflowing. Even mid-apology, he wants some credit for being lovable. It's an honest kind of mess. Regret and vanity share the same verse, and the song never sorts them out. By the second verse the posture drops. He's down on his knees, thirsty, running to her well, and the language turns toward scripture, the woman as water in a dry place.

Then the big gesture: "I'd swim the Mississippi river." It's the kind of vow soul singers have always made. But asked about that line, Bridges pointed to his family's roots in New Orleans and a father who moved to Atlanta for work, back to New Orleans, and finally to Texas. The impossible swim has a real map behind it.

The band plays all of this as if forgiveness might already be on its way. A shuffle rolls at an unhurried pace, the snare snapping the backbeat while a walking bass line strolls underneath. Clean electric guitar picks out arpeggiated chords, and a keyboard holds long chords that warm the edges. Bridges sings smooth and clear, never straining, and backing harmonies from Brittni Jessie, Tyesha Simpson, Ansley Dougherty and Njia Martin fill out the phrases. The room matters too. Niles City Sound in Fort Worth, founded by co-writers Chris Vivion, Austin Jenkins and Josh Block, works with eight-track tape and 70-year-old microphones, and the recording has that close, warm air.

Critics heard Sam Cooke and Otis Redding, and the debt is plain: the gospel-inflected plea, the sweetness laid over a sinner's admission. Bridges was once playing this on guitar to about ten people. When the demo surfaced on the Dallas blog Gorilla vs. Bear alongside "Coming Home," the response was huge, and a Columbia deal came within about six months.

What sticks is the gap between the size of the sin and the size of the ask, and the song lets you feel how badly someone can want a second chance while still hoping you'll notice their smile.

<genres>southern soul, retro soul, r&b</genres>

The narrator opens by saying he doesn't want much.
factCheck.note: The song opens with "I don't want much."

factCheck.claim: Lyric quote "Under perfume sheets" and nights out with the Jezebels
factCheck.note: The lyrics read "I was singing with them Jezebels / Under perfume sheets" and "All night long, I was out."

factCheck.claim: A golden smile, a heart overflowing
factCheck.note: Matches "Got a golden smile, heart overflowing."

factCheck.claim: In the second verse he is on his knees, thirsty, running to her well
factCheck.note: The lyrics give "down on my knees begging," "I thirst for you girl" and "running to your well" in the second verse. The scripture and water reading is interpretation.

factCheck.claim: Lyric quote: "I'd swim the Mississippi river"
"It's the kind of vow soul singers have always made."
factCheck.note: This is a claim about the history of soul and has no support. Reworded as a reading of the line itself.

factCheck.claim: Bridges pointed to his family's New Orleans roots and a father who moved to Atlanta, back to New Orleans, then Texas
factCheck.note: Matches the Current interview. The father's year back in New Orleans is left out, which does not change the account.
